# Can copper substitution tame the red dragon as record prices breathe new fire into debate? - As the price of copper heads ever skyward, the theme of substitution has come back to the forefront of market participants’ thinking. In this Insight we summarise the key drivers of substitution, highlighting where products have been substituted and what the future might hold. In short, will the rising price of copper, in particular relative to aluminium, ultimately cause demand destruction, snap the copper market back into balance and in doing so temper price appreciation? - Substitution away from copper currently results in a loss of around 2% of total demand each year, with this representing approximately 400,000 tonnes. Just over half of this loss is to aluminium, with the light metal gaining ground in particular in thermal conductivity applications rather than in electrical conductivity where copper’s supreme technical qualities will continue to favour its use. - Current record copper prices increasingly raise the prospect of an increase in substitution. A one percentage point increase in substitution would result in a loss of 1 million tonnes of copper demand by 2014. Significantly, by 2014 our base case copper forecast assumes prices start to soften as the market moves to a structural surplus, and as such any extra loss of demand would increase this surplus and further exacerbate downward price pressures. Copper Substitution ## Where are we now? It is first useful to have a look at the scale of substitution currently taking place. Using data from the International Copper Association since 2005, we can see that the overall volume of substitution away from copper increased year-on-year to 2007, before easing back thereafter. The percentages also follow a similar pattern, with substitution as a percentage of total copper demand peaking in 2007. One would expect the volumes to follow a similar pattern to overall demand for copper but what does the same pattern in the relative amount of substitution reveal? Perhaps very little, as more telling is the relative amount of substitution compared to the copper price. Unsurprisingly, there appears to be a relationship between high copper prices and substitution, linking to demand only indirectly because of the impact of demand on price. Indeed, the major rationale for swapping materials would be cost and the volatility of this cost, assuming that the technical qualities of competing materials are equivalent or in the absence of new technologies. #### **Gains and losses from substitution** 100

Metals Market Service Insight - February 2011 Page 2 of 5 Copper Substitution ## Money knocks on the door but technical qualities are the gatekeeper Generally it is the opportunity to save cash that is at the forefront of players’ minds when the issue of substitution comes up but clearly the alternative material has to be up to the job in hand. Can it perform at least as well or better? There are many considerations in this respect but ultimately it might simply come down to whether the new material can do the same thing without negative size or weight implications. For example, copper’s key technical advantage is its excellent electrical conductivity, although it is also a very good thermal conductor. For aluminium to achieve the same electrical conductivity as copper it would require a greater diameter of cable, thus needing more space, and possibly increasing costs, which could be impractical in a building but less so in areas where space is less of an issue. That is why there is little scope for substitution to aluminium in building wire and underground cables but why overhead power cables are largely made of aluminium. Among a raft of other considerations are legislation, redesign of parts to accommodate different technical qualities, retooling of machinery and retraining of staff and education of consumers on the merits of new materials. In order to jump through the apparent hoops of switching materials, there has to be a significant cost saving to be had, while this also needs to be large enough to cover the costs of the switchover. Moreover, there needs to be sufficient confidence that the cost saving will be maintained in future. The chart below shows that in 2007 when the volume of substitution and the percentage of substitution were highest in our data set there was both a high copper price and that the copper’s relative and nominal differential was high compared to its major substitute, aluminium. In 2009 we would imagine that firms shifted their focus away from innovation and more onto surviving the downturn. However, with copper prices at a record high, in addition to both the nominal and relative price difference with aluminium also at record levels, then this points to further substitution to come. #### **The copper price is important as is the relative and absolute difference to substitutes** 8000 4.00

## Substitution has favoured thermal conductive applications rather than electric Of the losses that copper has faced over the past few years over half has been to aluminium, with products mainly losing out in thermal conductivity applications, while optical fibre continues to expand its dominance in the telecom market. Other noteworthy trends are increased use of alloying agents, thus reducing the overall copper content. However, it is also important to remember that other related trends are also impacting demand including reducing the gauge of copper products. It is also worth noting where there hasn’t been much penetration and this is focussed in areas where copper’s supreme technical properties have won out. Most of this is focussed in the wire and cable sector and while we have seen penetration in telecom cable and overhead power cables, there is has been little impact in building wire. Here, barriers to substitution include the size and space of the conduit and even safety concerns that have resulted in legislation that demands copper and/or blocks aluminium’s use. In our view the area that faces the largest threat from substitution is commercial tube and heat exchanger material. Most automotive air conditioning and refrigeration (ACR) tube is already aluminium due to moves to reduce the weight of vehicles in a bid to make them more fuel efficient, although penetration into domestic and commercial air conditioning units is further behind. However, much more research into micro channel heat exchangers (MCHX) is also underway. Newly developed MCHX is manufactured with aluminium alloy rather than copper tube and there are reports that it has been used in trial air-conditioning production at Media, one of China’s largest air-conditioning manufacturers. If MCHX gains wider adoption in the AC industry it will dramatically reduce demand for ACR copper tube. In the wire and cable sector there is

less of a threat overall, given that copper will continue to dominate in the building wire segment, which is the top consumer of copper, although it does face a threat from copper clad aluminium wire in the power utility sector and from aluminium magnet wire. #### **Wire and cable dominates global demand for copper, although the smaller tube segment faces the biggest threat** 5% 8%

Metals Market Service Insight - February 2011 Page 4 of 5 Copper Substitution ## Auto and other drivers However, it is worth noting that the development of new applications could stem the tide at least to a degree. For example, the increasing prevalence of hybrid vehicles is boosting demand for copper as a typical hybrid car has two to three times the 22kg of copper that an average car contains. In addition, the increasing focus on green energy could also support demand as a result of copper use in wind turbines, for example. Moreover, other applications are being developed in as diverse areas as anti bacterial fittings in hospitals to fish nets in China. That is not the whole story though as there are other factors that come into play, for example, the increased use of scrap could also temper demand for refined metal by changing scrap’s mix in total demand. This is less likely in the wire and cable market but possible elsewhere. ### **Price cycles lower on demand destruction** While the threats outlined above do not present a doomsday scenario for copper demand, as even an increase in substitution to say 3% of the market from a peak of 2.3% in 2007 would represent around 750 thousand tonnes of our 2011 total demand estimate. However, it is too simplistic to knock this figure off our demand estimate for this year or next to get to a substitution adjusted demand forecast. It goes without saying that we already consider substitution within our demand forecasts so it would only be the incremental gain ahead of our expectations that could be taken off the top and not the total. This would be around 250 thousand tonnes off our 2011 estimate but significantly still leaves us in deficit this year. However, given that once material is substituted it is unlikely firms will switch back owing to the high costs of changing to a competing material, this could have implications further out in our forecast. If the current high price of copper does indeed increase the rate of substitution to 3% per year then this would represent a cumulative loss of a million tonnes of demand by 2014. By then copper prices are already forecast to have softened as the market moves to

a structural surplus, and increased substitution would further exacerbate downward price pressures. 

We currently expect cash quotes to average $9,700/t ($4.13/lb) in 2011 before ebbing lower in subsequent years as the market swings back into surplus in 2013 from the current year’s forecast deficit of over half a million tonnes.
